extracted.intended_audience: general readers; students and scholars of media/journalism; journalists and media critics
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate media (especially TV and online) that combine information and entertainment (infotainment/soft news), by recognizing their defining features, production techniques, impacts, and criticisms. Useful for media studies, journalism criticism, and newsroom practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: information + entertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: Infotainment, a portmanteau of information and entertainment, is a type of media, usually television or online, that provides a combination of information and entertainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically applied to formats that blend news/information with entertainment elements; the term is sometimes used disparagingly to devalue such content relative to 'hard news'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entertaining nature and production techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Infotainment can generally be identified by its entertaining nature. Infotainment may also involve the use of flashy graphics, fast-paced editing, music, sensationalism, and sometimes satire to catch the viewer/readers' attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for stylistic choices (graphics, editing, music) and tone (sensational, humorous, personality-driven) that prioritize attention and entertainment; examples include Larry King Live, Entertainment Tonight, The Daily Show, The Oprah Winfrey Show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soft news vs hard news characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: It is also called soft news as a way to distinguish it from serious journalism or hard news; soft news is described as 'more personality-centered, less time-bound, more practical, and more incident-based than other news.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess stories on whether they emphasize personalities and practical tips versus breaking events, public affairs, or systemic issues to classify them on the soft/hard spectrum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topicality and timeliness as a hardness measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Some authors use only the topicality and timeliness aspects of a story to determine whether news is hard news or soft news; the more topical and timely, the 'harder' and more serious the news is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate immediacy and current relevance: breaking, time-sensitive coverage tends to be hard news; evergreen or advisory pieces tend toward infotainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schramm's delayed reward vs immediate reward classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Wilbur Schramm separated news into a delayed reward class (including news of public affairs, economic matters, social problems, science, education and health), which closely resembles hard news, and an immediate reward class (including news of crime/corruption, accidents and disasters, sports, social events, and human interest) which closely resembles infotainment/soft news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify content by whether it offers longer-term civic value ('delayed reward') or immediate emotional/entertainment payoff ('immediate reward').

rubrics_metrics.name: "News you can use" / tips-and-advice placement
rubrics_metrics.description: 'News you can use', a common marketing phrase highlighting a specific genre of journalism, spans the gray area. Tips, advice and hobby-based news fall at the infotainment end of this genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize 'practical tip' or lifestyle formats as likely infotainment even if they provide useful information to individuals; importance is subjective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive informational value (or lack thereof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most infotainment television programs on networks and broadcast cable only contain general information on the subjects they cover and may not be considered to have high levels of substantive informational value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate depth and verifiability of information: shallow, general coverage indicates lower substantive value and leans toward infotainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing accusations without verifiable evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: An infotainment broadcast may frame accusations of a celebrity or other individual committing a crime as a reality, with no verifiable factual support or evidence of such claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for presentation of allegations as fact without sourcing or verification — a key anti-pattern of infotainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalism and celebrity-driven triviality
rubrics_metrics.description: Infotainment 'seems to hurtle from one event to another, often dwelling on trivial, celebrity-driven content.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spot prioritization of celebrity, scandal, or shock value over public-interest reporting as an indicator of infotainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dilution of hard news with fiction/drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Today's broadcasting of what is considered 'hard' informative news is sometimes diluted with attributes of fiction or drama, and infotainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate news presentations that adopt dramatic storytelling or fictionalized elements—these can blur the line and reduce informational rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership influence and commercial incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Some argue that a catalyst for infotainment may be the acquisition of major news networks by conglomerates primarily based in the entertainment business; the ownership structure can be traced using infotainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider corporate ownership and cross-business incentives (e.g., parent company film/TV interests) as drivers that shape editorial choices toward infotainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commodification and exploitation of personal tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Some forms of infotainment can commodify real people through their personal tragedies or scandals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether coverage objectifies, sensationalizes, or monetizes individuals' suffering rather than treating subjects with dignity and public-interest context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infotainers: personalities crossing journalism/entertainment line
rubrics_metrics.description: Infotainers are entertainers in infotainment media, such as news anchors or satirists who cross the line between journalism (quasi-journalism) and entertainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify hosts/personalities whose performance and celebrity status overshadow informational duties; examples include Barbara Walters, Oprah Winfrey, Jon Stewart, Bill O’Reilly, Rachel Maddow, Alex Jones, Geraldo Rivera.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media amplification and participatory production
rubrics_metrics.description: Infotainment is now able to reach an ever-growing audience through the widespread popularity and use of social media applications; the interactive nature has allowed consumers of infotainment to become producers, generating their own news and commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how platform mechanics (sharing, virality, user-generated content) amplify infotainment and how journalists may repurpose such content without sufficient verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity and lack of precise consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: A precise academic consensus on the definition of what constitutes infotainment/soft news as opposed to hard news has not yet been reached. Many authors have commented that the ideas 'are often not clearly defined or not defined at all.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat classifications as interpretive and context-dependent; multiple operationalizations exist in scholarship and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on audience attention and editorial choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Local news broadcasters are more regularly covering local events in a way that provokes entertainment in viewers, with arresting footage, animated visuals, and rhetorical headlines that generate opinions; the media's ability to tell and sell stories allows them to not only to document tragedy, but to misrepresent or exploit it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider attention-economy incentives (clickbait, headlines, visuals) and their ethical implications when evaluating whether content serves public information needs or merely seeks engagement.
